newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: The 10-year French bond future moved into positive territory in after-hours trade on Friday on GLOBEX after EU ministers announced a deal to enforce budgetary discipline after the launch of a single European currency.

The notionnel clawed back most of its losses late in the daytime session, propelled by a firmer U.S. Treasuries market. The 10-year notionnel settled down 20 basis points at 128.02 after touching a low earlier in the day of 127.46
Analysts said the EU pact eased pressure on the market but that the key influence short-term still was the United States.
If the T-Bond closes higher, Christian Sene, technical analyst at BNP, said the March notionnel contract could retest the highs it hit at the start of the week of 129.18.

The franc jumped on the news of the EU pact, trading at 3.3745 per mark at 1640 GMT, up a third of a centime from before the deal. German finance minister Theo Waigel called the stability a "credible signal the euro will be a hard currency."

Analysts, however, said it smacked of compromise. Valerie Plagnol, chief strategist at Credit Commercial de France, said "it's definitely not as hard as the Germans were asking for, it looks to be more of a compromise agreement."

Analysts said the agreement, however, was still bullish for European convergence. "but we need to see more detail about the kind of fines and how automatic implementation works in practice, Plagnol said.
PIBOR extended its gains on GLOBEX after settling three basis points higher in anticipation of a deal in Dublin which trades hope will pave the way for further rate cuts.

Analysts also saw positive news from President Jacques Chirac's televised comments on Thursday in which he reiterated his commitment to a single currency and deficit-cutting and ruled out a cabinet reshuffle.
"The results can be summarised as follows: no policy change, reforms will go on," said economist Eric Chaney of Morgan Stanley. "This is probably the most important for investors."
He said Chirac's pledge to steer a steady course meant that the franc-mark parity would not be questioned by the government.

"The most obvious conclusion of all this is that Mr Chirac's words were sweet for the short end of the yield curve," Chaney said. "The spectre of a confidence crisis which resulted in high risk premia on French assets has practically vanished."
Chaney said the Bank of France should find more arguments in Chirac's "orthodox credo" to ease rates with inflation at 1.5 percent and likely to fall more in months ahead.

He said the Bank had room, however, only to shave 20 basis points off its key intervention rate as long as the Bundesbank keeps its repo rate at three percent, barring a "mini-revolution" modifying the hawkish makeup of the monetary policy council when two members retire at year end.
But the overall market focus would still likely to be overseas. "The U.S. is increasingly capturing the focus," said Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais.
"In a more global sense, equity markets are also a cause for concern," he added. "Any slide in equity markets that snowballs could trigger selling pressure on the bond markets."
